newsitem.title: UK: SWIMMING-ELITE EUROPEANS FACE FIRST MAJOR TEST SINCE OLYMPICS.
newsitem.headline: SWIMMING-ELITE EUROPEANS FACE FIRST MAJOR TEST SINCE OLYMPICS.

text.p: European swimmers face their first big events since the Olympics this weekend with 38 finals crammed into three days of the inaugural European sprint and short-course championships.
The 25-metre Neptun pool in the former East German city of Rostock stages the races which, in the absence of all the Atlanta gold medallists, should be dominated by Germany.

With world champion Franziska van Almsick among the missing, Sandra Voelker leads the German challenge, seeking to increase her collection of 12 European sprint championship golds, Olympic silver at 100 freestyle and bronze at 50 freestyle.
The preliminaries begin on Thursday with heats in two distance events before the real action gets under way on Friday.

Olympic champions have stayed away because they face an array of international championships over the next 13 months -- world short-course in Gothenburg in April, European long-course in Seville in August and world long-course in Perth in January 1998, as well as the World Cup series over the next two months.

Alexander Popov, knifed in a Moscow street last August a month after achieving a unique Olympic feat in Atlanta, has returned to his base in Australia hoping his incomparable powers have not been irreparably diminished.

Popov, the only swimmer to have won the 50 and 100 metres freestyle at successive Olympics, and Denis Pankratov, Atlanta gold medallist at 100 and 200 butterfly, are the most prominent absentees from a Russian team of just four swimmers.

Hungary's elite squad traditionally shuns short-course meetings. Thus Norbert Rozsa and Attila Czene, Olympic champions at 200 breaststroke and 200 individual medley respectively, will not compete while Krisztina Egerszegi, who won her third successive 200 backstroke Olympic gold in Atlanta, has retired anyway.
Ireland's Michelle Smith, triple Olympic champion in Atlanta's Georgia Tech pool, and Belgium's 100 breaststroke gold medallist Frederik Deburghgraeve have also passed up Rostock.
In the meantime the versatile Voelker, competing in five individual events, faces tough duels in two of them -- 50 butterfly and 50 backstroke -- with her former Hamburg team mate Antje Buschschulte.
Buschschulte, 17, finished just 0.03 seconds behind Voelker in the 50 butterfly in the German short-course championships two weekends ago and both were just outside European record time.

Van Almsick, who recently left her longstanding coach Dieter Lindemann, is aiming for Olympic gold in Sydney in 2000 after being denied her ambition in Atlanta by Costa Rica's Claudia Poll in the 200 freestyle.
But neither van Almsick nor fellow former East German Dagmar Hase, the 1992 Olympic 400 freestyle champion who has gone back on her decision to retire after Atlanta, is competing in Rostock.

Sylvia Gerasch, 100 breaststroke world champion back in 1986, returns to international competition after two years suspension for excessive levels of caffeine which the former East German attributed to drinking coffee.

Her breaststroke opponents include Poland's Alicja Peczak, who also served a ban for a positive dope test but has since collected bronze medals at both the European long-course and world short-course championships in 1995.

Britain look to Mark Foster, 1993 world short-course 50 freestyle champion and current 50 butterfly world record holder, and distance freestyler Ian Wilson and backstroker Neil Willey, who both collected silver medals at the 1995 world short-course championships in Rio de Janeiro.

The meeting links the old sprint championships -- held four times from 1991 to 1994 and comprising 50-metre races in all four strokes, 100 individual medley and 4x50 relays -- with all the races in the Olympic programme bar relays.
Prize-money of 5,000 marks ($3,210) is on offer for European records to the 250 swimmers from 30 nations.
